title: Electing a House Speaker Once Took 133 Ballots
description:
Hakeem Jeffries is in the news this week as House Democrats' nominee for Speaker. Electing a Speaker usually takes one vote. In 1855 it took two months and 133 ballots, the longest Speaker election in American history.
🚶 Visiting San Diego? Explore its history on a guided tour with Fable: https://fablehospitality.com

Every frame is drawn with code. No stock footage, no AI video.

0:00 Speaker of the House
0:05 Usually one vote. In 1855, two months
0:10 December 3, 1855: the old Hall of the House
0:15 A country splitting over slavery
0:19 Ballot No. 1: about twenty names, no majority
0:24 Christmas, New Year's, ballot after ballot
0:28 The all-night session
0:33 Horace Greeley attacked
0:38 February 2, 1856: the plurality rule
0:43 Ballot No. 133: Banks 103, Aiken 100
0:50 Still the record
0:54 2023: fifteen ballots
0:59 One ballot is the easy version

Note: the 34th Congress met on December 3, 1855, in the old Hall of the House (today's National Statuary Hall; the House moved to its current chamber in 1857). On February 2, 1856, the House adopted a plurality rule, and Nathaniel P. Banks of Massachusetts won on the 133rd ballot with 103 votes to 100 for William Aiken of South Carolina. Sources give 17 to 21 candidates receiving votes on the first day, so the video says "about twenty". The all-night session of January 9-10, 1856 lasted about 18 hours. Rep. Albert Rust of Arkansas assaulted New York Tribune editor Horace Greeley in Washington in late January 1856. The 15 ballots of January 2023 were the most since 1859-60.

Images (public domain): "The House of Representatives" by Samuel F. B. Morse (1822, via Wikimedia Commons); "The Capitol, at Washington — East Front" and "Statuary Hall" from Joseph West Moore, Picturesque Washington (1887, Internet Archive); portrait of Horace Greeley from James Parton, The Life of Horace Greeley (1855, Internet Archive); portrait of N. P. Banks from Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, vol. 1 (1887, Internet Archive). Ballots, calendar pages and documents drawn in code.
Maps drawn in code from Natural Earth (world-atlas) and US Census (us-atlas) outlines.
Narration voice is synthetic.
